rewrite.description: Old News keeps The Steel Woods' heavy riffing intact while sharpening the band's storytelling on songs about addiction, mortality and hard-won faith. Big, twin-guitar Southern rock arrangements carry gravelly, full-throated vocals. It is a strong second album and a natural companion to the debut.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to V28's Southern-rock lineage, with deepening Americana songwriting; oriented toward mainstream rock/Americana audiences rather than the Core.

problems: lineage phrased as fact though Inferred

rewrite.lineage: Sounds like a blues-rock-leaning branch of V28's Southern guitar-rock lineage, indebted in particular to Allman Brothers-style slide guitar, heading toward the contemporary blues-rock circuit rather than the punk-adjacent Core.

rewrite.description: Blood Harmony pairs the Lovell sisters' close harmonies and slide-guitar riffing with some of the band's most polished, big-room production. The songs lean on stomping blues-rock grooves and hooky choruses rather than long jams. A strong recent landmark for the blues-rock wing of Southern rock's mainstream continuation.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Larkin Poe's slide-guitar blues-rock, which sounds indebted to V28's Southern guitar lineage; distinct from both the boogie-rock (Blackberry Smoke) and jam-band (Allman Betts) wings of the same lane.

rewrite.description: Musgraves' major-label debut is wry, plainspoken country songwriting about small-town Texas life, weed jokes and quiet rebellion, set to a traditional pedal-steel-and-fiddle Nashville sound. It came from inside the mainstream country machine yet read as an outsider's record, ahead of the pop crossover that followed. A clean entry point for how a country insider can read as an indie-friendly songwriter.
rewrite.lineage: Made within mainstream Nashville (X1), with a plainspoken, Cosmic American-leaning songwriting voice that sounds indebted to V21; leads forward into Musgraves' own pop-crossover arc rather than toward the Core scene.

problems: unsupported causal influence claim on later records

rewrite.description: Musgraves' pivot record folds disco shimmer and vocoder into her pedal-steel country base, trading jokes for a wide-open, in-love glow. It anticipated the 'country as mode' crossover wave that Cowboy Carter and Post Malone's country turn later took to pop scale. Essential for hearing how far the genre's edges can stretch while keeping a steel guitar in the mix.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds like a split from the mainstream-Nashville/Cosmic American line (X1/V21) toward adult-pop production; the branch resembles later 2020s pop-country crossovers like Cowboy Carter and F-1 Trillion rather than the indie-twang Core.

rewrite.description: A masked, mysterious persona singing lonesome-cowboy ballads over reverb-heavy Telecaster twang and hazy, echoing production, closer to Chris Isaak or Roy Orbison than to Nashville radio. Released on indie stalwart Sub Pop rather than a country label, it is the clearest 'indie artist adopts country iconography' landmark of the 2010s. Good starting point for the queer, theatrical branch of the country-turn trend.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to country's outlaw-and-crooner imagery (X1) filtered through the indie label system rather than the twang scene proper; his branch continues through Bronco and Stampede rather than into Core indie twang.

rewrite.description: A major-label-scaled follow-up to Pony, trading some of the debut's mystery for widescreen, string-and-pedal-steel Americana and a fuller band sound. It shows the country-turn persona graduating from cult indie status to a bigger pop stage. Representative of how far the Peck project moved from Sub Pop-scale intimacy toward mainstream country crossover.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Peck's outlaw-persona sound, which draws on mainstream country imagery (X1), into major-label pop-country territory; does not feed back into the indie-twang Core.
Sounds indebted to mainstream country's confessional songwriting mode (X1), seen through an Irish indie-pop lens; leads onward through CMAT's own catalog rather than into the twang Core.

rewrite.description: CMAT's second album widens the scope with orchestral flourishes and even bigger country-pop hooks while keeping the same sardonic, oversharing lyric style about family and disastrous romance. Her big, theatrical voice rides string swells and twangy guitar without losing the jokes. A strong second landmark showing the persona maturing beyond the debut's novelty framing.
rewrite.lineage: Continues CMAT's country-pop, which sounds indebted to mainstream country songwriting (X1), toward arena-pop scale; stays in the pop-country lane rather than joining indie twang.

rewrite.description: CMAT's third album leans further into arena-scaled country-pop with sardonic, sometimes political lyrics about Ireland and modern life. Big choruses and country signifiers sit alongside confessional, funny-sad storytelling delivered in her broad, theatrical voice. It is the newest and most outward-looking entry in her pop-country run.
rewrite.lineage: Continues CMAT's pop-country branch, which sounds indebted to mainstream country songwriting (X1); the newest data point in the trend, feeding forward rather than back toward the Core.

problems: lineage framing is interpretive, marked Documented

rewrite.lineage: Positions itself against mainstream Nashville country (X1) and its sidelining of Black artists, drawing in elder figures like Linda Martell; the branch runs forward into pop and country radio rather than into indie twang.

problems: Wikipedia and Josh Terry cited as authority

rewrite.description: Mitski strips back her usual intensity for a hushed, string-laden record with Americana, country and folk inflections, closer to spare orchestral pop than any Nashville sound. Her voice sits low and close against swelling strings and choir, reining in the pop impulses of her earlier work. It is a borderline but real example of an indie-pop artist reaching toward country/Americana textures rather than a country record proper.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Americana and country folk's spare, string-backed songwriting (adjacent to X1/V21 territory), filtered through Mitski's indie-rock background; the branch stays within her own art-pop catalog rather than feeding the Core scene.

rewrite.description: The hip-hop/pop star's full turn to country, built on duets with Nashville names such as Morgan Wallen and Blake Shelton over pedal steel and Telecaster twang, marking his rebrand as a Nashville-adjacent artist. It is a major 'pop artist becomes country artist' moment of the mid-2020s, running parallel to Cowboy Carter. A useful landmark for the sheer scale of mainstream pop's country pivot.
rewrite.lineage: Plugs directly into mainstream Nashville duet culture (X1) through its guest list, with outlaw-country signifiers that are more resemblance than lineage; leads forward into country radio rather than into the indie twang Core.

rewrite.description: A spare, dulcimer-and-piano confessional record that became a defining Laurel Canyon singer-songwriter statement, all raw diary-entry lyrics and an unmistakable soaring voice. It set an emotional-honesty template that generations of confessional songwriters worked from. The clearest entry point into the LA scene this lane covers.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds rooted in the folk-revival songwriting that also fed Cosmic American Music (V21) and Dylan/The Band's roots turn (V22); its confessional line runs forward into mainstream singer-songwriter pop rather than into the twang-scene Core.

rewrite.description: Mitchell's commercial peak folds jazz-tinged arrangements and studio-band polish into her songwriting, moving the Laurel Canyon sound toward smoother, LA-studio sophistication. It works as a bridge between confessional folk and the soft-rock mainstream of the mid-'70s. Representative of how far the scene's polish could stretch without losing songwriting depth.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Mitchell's folk-rock songwriting, rooted in V21/V22-adjacent traditions, toward jazz-pop sophistication; sounds closer to the smoothed-out LA session sound than to country rock's twang.

Extends Mitchell's folk-rock songwriting (V21/V22-adjacent) into jazz-fusion territory; a dead end for country-rock purposes, though its drifting art-folk sound is echoed by later songwriters outside the Core.

problems: lineage should cite concrete shared members

rewrite.description: Former members of the Byrds, Buffalo Springfield and the Hollies lock their voices into the three-part harmony blueprint of Laurel Canyon folk rock, built on warm acoustic fingerpicking and easygoing tempos. It is the founding document of the harmony sound before Neil Young joined for the electrified CSNY records already covered in the Core lineage. Essential for hearing the vocal-harmony half of the scene distinct from Young's guitar side.
rewrite.lineage: Formed by David Crosby (the Byrds), Stephen Stills (Buffalo Springfield) and Graham Nash (the Hollies), directly linking it to the folk-rock lineage behind V21, with Young's later arrival tying it to V20; this harmony branch leads into the LA soft-rock mainstream rather than the twangier Core sound.

rewrite.description: Browne's stark, piano-and-guitar meditations on failing relationships and mortality set the introspective, plainly sung template for LA singer-songwriter rock, with David Lindley's slide and fiddle coloring the arrangements. It sits alongside Blue as a high point of the confessional Laurel Canyon songwriter mode. A strong entry point for the lane's more melancholy, less country-inflected side.
rewrite.lineage: Browne co-wrote the Eagles' 'Take It Easy', tying him to the same LA country-rock circle (V21) as the Eagles and Linda Ronstadt; his own records stay within the soft-rock singer-songwriter mainstream rather than crossing into twangier Core territory.
Continues Browne's Laurel Canyon songwriting, close to the Cosmic American circle (V21), into fuller studio-pop arrangements; sounds firmly of the soft-rock mainstream rather than the Core.
Extends Browne's Laurel Canyon songwriting (V21-adjacent) into a road-diary live format; stays outside the Core twang scene.

problems: vague/uncertain personnel phrasing and pedal steel claim

rewrite.description: The Eagles' debut, with former Flying Burrito Brother Bernie Leadon and ex-Poco bassist Randy Meisner in the lineup, applies tight vocal harmonies and banjo-flecked twang to concise, radio-ready country-rock songs. It shows the Cosmic American Music circle scaling the sound down into hit singles. A useful landmark for how country rock's rougher edges got smoothed into mainstream pop.
rewrite.lineage: Splits directly from the Cosmic American Music/country-rock lineage (V21) through shared members from the Flying Burrito Brothers and Poco, trading V21's rawer twang for tighter pop songcraft; leads forward into the soft-rock mainstream rather than the Core.

rewrite.description: Ronstadt's commercial breakthrough pairs her powerhouse voice with a crack LA studio band, covering country, pop and rock songs in a lush, pedal-steel-backed style. It became a model for the polished, interpretive side of country rock distinct from songwriter-driven records. A key landmark for how a covers-based singer could anchor the scene's sound.
rewrite.lineage: Tied to V21's country-rock network: Glenn Frey and Don Henley played in Ronstadt's backing band before forming the Eagles; her interpretive, hit-single approach leads into mainstream pop-country rather than the twang Core.

rewrite.description: Ronstadt continues her interpretive country-rock approach with covers of Warren Zevon, Buddy Holly, Roy Orbison and the Rolling Stones, sung with full-throated power over polished LA studio arrangements. It epitomizes the late-'70s soft-rock mainstream at its commercial peak. Good second landmark for the covers-and-craft half of the lane.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Ronstadt's covers-based country rock, rooted in the V21 scene; sounds squarely of the mainstream pop-country lane rather than feeding the Core.

problems: lineage mixes documented ties with resemblance

rewrite.description: Nilsson's biggest commercial hit mixes barroom piano ballads, a hit cover ('Without You') and eccentric studio pop, sitting just outside the singer-songwriter mainstream of his LA peers thanks to his theatrical voice and studio-rat production choices. It shows the LA scene's more idiosyncratic, less country-adjacent wing. Useful contrast to the straighter country-rock records in this lane.
rewrite.lineage: Runs parallel to the Laurel Canyon songwriter scene (V21/V22-adjacent) rather than descending from country rock; his documented ties are to Randy Newman, whose songs he recorded on Nilsson Sings Newman, and to the Beatles, and the branch leads into orchestral pop rather than toward the Core.
